topics.name: Introduction to Python
subtopics: History and Use Cases of Python

questions.title: Personal Greeting Line
questions.description:
Your first Python script greets a user by name, just like the classic program every beginner runs after installing the interpreter.

Input Format:
One line containing a person's name.

Output Format:
Print exactly: Hello, <name>! Welcome to Python.

Constraints:
The name has 1 to 50 characters and may contain letters and spaces.
questions.sampleoutput2: Hello, Ada Lovelace! Welcome to Python.
questions.output2: Hello, Grace Hopper! Welcome to Python.
questions.sourcecode:
name = input()
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to Python.")

questions.title: Separator Drill Print
questions.description:
A small formatting drill for the print function's sep parameter: read two words and a separator character, then print the words glued together by that character.

Input Format:
Line 1: first word.
Line 2: second word.
Line 3: a single separator character.

Output Format:
One line: word1 and word2 joined by the separator character.

Constraints:
Each word has 1 to 20 characters; the separator is one non-space character.
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= len(word) <= 20, separator is one non-space character
questions.sourcecode:
a = input()
b = input()
sep = input()
print(a, b, sep=sep)

questions.title: Age Next Year
questions.description:
A school registration script reports how old a student will be next year.

Input Format:
One line: a single-word name and an integer age separated by a space.

Output Format:
Print exactly: <name> will turn <age + 1> next year.

Constraints:
1 <= age <= 120; the name is one word.
questions.sourcecode:
name, age = input().split()
age = int(age)
print(f"{name} will turn {age + 1} next year.")

questions.title: Two Number Math Lines
questions.description:
A tiny calculator drill prints the sum, difference and product of two integers, one result per line.

Input Format:
One line: two integers a and b separated by a space.

Output Format:
Three lines: a + b, then a - b, then a * b.

Constraints:
-1000 <= a, b <= 1000.
questions.sourcecode:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
print(a + b)
print(a - b)
print(a * b)

questions.title: Version String Builder
questions.description:
A version-reporting drill builds a full Python version string from its three numeric parts, the way python3 --version reports it.

Input Format:
One line: three integers major, minor and patch separated by spaces.

Output Format:
Line 1: Python <major>.<minor>.<patch>
Line 2: Checking interpreter: python<major>

Constraints:
0 <= major <= 9; 0 <= minor <= 99; 0 <= patch <= 99.
questions.sourcecode:
major, minor, patch = map(int, input().split())
print(f"Python {major}.{minor}.{patch}")
print(f"Checking interpreter: python{major}")

questions.title: Two Decimal Price Printer
questions.description:
Money values must always be shown with exactly two decimal places. This drill reads a price and prints it in that fixed format using an f-string.

Input Format:
One line: a price value (it may have any number of decimal digits, or none).

Output Format:
The price formatted to exactly 2 decimal places.

Constraints:
0 <= price <= 100000.
questions.sourcecode:
price = float(input())
print(f"{price:.2f}")

questions.title: Cinema Ticket Booking Slip
questions.description:
A cinema counter runs a small Python script that prints a booking slip line whenever a customer reserves a seat for a movie.

Input Format:
Line 1: customer name.
Line 2: movie title (may contain spaces).

Output Format:
Print exactly: <name> booked a ticket for <movie>.

Constraints:
The name and the title have 1 to 40 characters each.
questions.subtopic: History and Use Cases of Python
questions.sampleoutput1: Maya booked a ticket for Dune Part Two.
questions.sampleoutput2: Dev booked a ticket for Inception.
questions.output1: Aisha booked a ticket for Interstellar.
questions.output2: Rohan booked a ticket for 3 Idiots.
questions.output3: Nina booked a ticket for Tenet.
questions.sourcecode:
name = input()
movie = input()
print(f"{name} booked a ticket for {movie}.")

questions.title: Food Delivery Order Confirmation
questions.description:
A food delivery app confirms an order with one formatted line showing the dish and its price.

Input Format:
Line 1: dish name (may contain spaces).
Line 2: price as a decimal number.

Output Format:
Print exactly: Order confirmed: <dish> for Rs. <price> where <price> has exactly 2 decimal places.

Constraints:
0 <= price <= 10000.
questions.subtopic: History and Use Cases of Python
questions.sampleoutput1: Order confirmed: Paneer Butter Masala for Rs. 8.50
questions.sampleoutput2: Order confirmed: Veg Fried Rice for Rs. 12.00
questions.output1: Order confirmed: Margherita Pizza for Rs. 9.99
questions.output2: Order confirmed: Masala Dosa for Rs. 4.75
questions.output3: Order confirmed: Chocolate Cake for Rs. 15.50

dish = input()
price = float(input())
print(f"Order confirmed: {dish} for Rs. {price:.2f}")

questions.title: City Weather Report Line
questions.description:
A weather widget prints one report line per city from its latest temperature reading.

Input Format:
Line 1: city name.
Line 2: temperature as an integer in degrees Celsius.

Output Format:
Print exactly: Weather in <city>: <temp>C

Constraints:
-50 <= temp <= 60.
questions.subtopic: History and Use Cases of Python
questions.sourcecode:
city = input()
temp = int(input())
print(f"Weather in {city}: {temp}C")

questions.title: Library Shelf Update
questions.description:
A librarian's helper script logs every donation of books to the shelves.

Input Format:
Line 1: book title (may contain spaces).
Line 2: number of copies as an integer.

Output Format:
Print exactly: Added <copies> copies of <title> to the library.

Constraints:
1 <= copies <= 100.
questions.subtopic: History and Use Cases of Python
questions.sampleoutput1: Added 3 copies of Clean Code to the library.
questions.sampleoutput2: Added 5 copies of Automate the Boring Stuff to the library.
questions.output1: Added 2 copies of Fluent Python to the library.
questions.output2: Added 10 copies of Atomic Habits to the library.

copies = int(input())
print(f"Added {copies} copies of {title} to the library.")

questions.title: Py2 vs Py3 Division Report
questions.description:
A compatibility teaching tool shows how the same division behaves differently across Python versions. Given a and b, print the Python 3 true-division value and the value Python 2 would give for dividing the integers a and b, which rounds toward negative infinity (the floor of the true quotient).

Input Format:
One line: two integers a and b separated by a space (b is never 0).

Output Format:
Line 1: py3: <a / b formatted to exactly 2 decimals>
Line 2: py2: <floor of a divided by b, printed as an integer>

Constraints:
-1000 <= a, b <= 1000; b != 0.
questions.sourcecode:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
print(f"py3: {a / b:.2f}")
print(f"py2: {a // b}")

questions.title: Command Line Rebuilder
questions.description:
A launcher utility stores a command as its name plus argument tokens and rebuilds the exact command line for its audit log.

Input Format:
Line 1: the command name (one word).
Line 2: the number of arguments n.
Line 3: n argument tokens separated by single spaces.

Output Format:
Line 1: the full command line: the name followed by the arguments, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: Args: <n>

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 10; each token has 1 to 20 characters.
questions.sourcecode:
cmd = input()
n = int(input())
line = cmd
for token in input().split():
    line = line + " " + token
print(line)
print(f"Args: {n}")

questions.title: Tiny Variable Simulator
questions.description:
A teacher replays a beginner's first REPL session. The session manipulates a single variable named x and prints it on request.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of session lines. Then n lines, each one of:
- x = <int>  (assign x)
- x = x + <int>  (increase x)
- x = x * <int>  (multiply x)
- print  (output the current value of x)

Output Format:
One line per print statement showing the current value of x.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 20; all values are integers with absolute value at most 100; x is assigned before any arithmetic; at least one print appears.
questions.sampleinput1:
4
x = 7
x = x + 3
print
x = x * 2
questions.input1:
5
x = 2
x = x * 6
print
x = x + 1
print
questions.input3:
6
x = 1
x = x + 2
x = x * 3
x = x + 4
x = x * 5
print

questions.title: Code Point Explorer
questions.description:
Python 3 strings are Unicode, unlike the byte-oriented ASCII str of Python 2. A teacher script proves it by printing every character's Unicode code point.

Input Format:
One line: a word made of letters only.

Output Format:
One line per character: <char> -> <code point>
Then a final line: Total: <sum of all the code points>

Constraints:
1 <= len(word) <= 15; letters only.
questions.sourcecode:
word = input()
total = 0
for ch in word:
    print(f"{ch} -> {ord(ch)}")
    total = total + ord(ch)
print(f"Total: {total}")

questions.title: Release Era Ladder
questions.description:
A history quiz app asks which major Python version line was current in a given year. Use these ranges: 1991-1993 -> 0.9, 1994-1999 -> 1.0, 2000-2007 -> 2.0, 2008 and later -> 3.0.

Input Format:
One line: a year Y.

Output Format:
Print exactly: Year <Y>: Python <version>

Constraints:
1991 <= Y <= 2020.

questions.title: Print Statement Translator
questions.description:
A migration helper rewrites Python 2 print statements into Python 3 calls. Remember: a trailing comma in Python 2 suppressed the newline and printed a trailing space, which becomes end=" " in Python 3.

Input Format:
Line 1: n. Then n lines, each a Python 2 statement of the form print ARG where ARG is a double-quoted string, a bare identifier or an integer, optionally followed by a trailing comma.

Output Format:
For each statement print its Python 3 equivalent: print(ARG) normally, or print(ARG, end=" ") when the original had a trailing comma.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 10; each ARG has 1 to 20 characters.

questions.title: Variable Store Simulator
questions.description:
Simulate a beginner's variable store: named boxes that hold integers, supporting assignments, updates, lookups and deletion.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of commands. Then n commands, one per line:
- set NAME V  (store V under NAME)
- add NAME V  (add V to NAME; if NAME does not exist yet, create it with value V)
- show NAME  (print NAME = value)
- show all  (print all stored names sorted alphabetically, space separated, or EMPTY if none)
- delete NAME  (remove NAME; NAME is guaranteed to exist)

Output Format:
One line per show command as described above.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 30; names are single lowercase words; -1000 <= V <= 1000.
questions.sampleinput1:
7
set count 5
set total 12
add count 3
show count
show all
delete total
show all
questions.sampleinput2:
5
set a 1
set b 2
show all
delete a
show all
questions.input1:
4
set score 10
add score 90
show score
show all
questions.input2:
3
add bonus 7
show bonus
show all
questions.input3:
4
set m 4
delete m
show all
set m -2
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= n <= 30, -1000 <= V <= 1000, names are lowercase words

questions.title: Migration Compatibility Checker
questions.description:
A migration scanner reads the lines of a small script and flags every Python 2-only print statement. A line needs migration exactly when it is 'print' alone or starts with 'print ' (the word print followed by a space). Lines like print(x) or print("hi") are already Python 3 compatible.

Input Format:
Line 1: n. Then n non-empty lines of a script (each at most 60 characters).

Output Format:
For each line, print '<line number>: MIGRATE' or '<line number>: OK' (line numbers start at 1). Then print '<migrated> of <n> lines need migration'.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 15; each line is 1 to 60 characters.
questions.sampleoutput1:
1: MIGRATE
2: OK
3: OK
4: MIGRATE
2 of 4 lines need migration
questions.sampleoutput2:
1: OK
2: OK
3: OK
0 of 3 lines need migration
questions.output1:
1: MIGRATE
2: MIGRATE
3: OK
2 of 3 lines need migration
questions.output2:
1: OK
2: MIGRATE
1 of 2 lines need migration
questions.input3:
5
print(1)
print "x"
print(x, y)
print  result
print

2: MIGRATE
3: OK

questions.title: Script Run Log Analyzer
questions.description:
A CI runner logs executions of Python practice scripts and needs a summary report.

Input Format:
Line 1: n. Then n lines: STATUS NAME TIME where STATUS is OK or FAIL, NAME is a single-token script name and TIME is the run duration in seconds (a decimal number).

Output Format:
Line 1: Total runs: <n>
Line 2: Passed: <count of OK runs>
Line 3: Failed: <count of FAIL runs>
Line 4: Slowest: <name> (<time with 2 decimals>s) for the run with the largest TIME; if several runs tie, use the earliest one in the log.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 20; 0.1 <= TIME <= 99.9.
questions.sampleinput1:
4
OK etl.py 1.5
FAIL scraper.py 3.2
OK quiz.py 0.8
OK etl.py 2.0
questions.sampleoutput1:
Total runs: 4
Passed: 3
Failed: 1
Slowest: scraper.py (3.20s)
questions.sampleinput2:
3
OK a.py 2.5
FAIL b.py 2.5
OK c.py 1.0
questions.sampleoutput2:
Total runs: 3
Passed: 2
Failed: 1
Slowest: a.py (2.50s)
questions.output1:
Total runs: 2
Passed: 1
Failed: 1
Slowest: y2 (0.20s)
questions.output2:
Total runs: 1
Passed: 1
Failed: 0
Slowest: solo.py (9.99s)
questions.input3:
5
FAIL f1 10.05
OK f2 10.04
OK f3 10.05
FAIL f4 9.5
OK f5 1.0
questions.output3:
Total runs: 5
Passed: 3
Failed: 2
Slowest: f1 (10.05s)
questions.sourcecode:
def main():
    n = int(input())
    passed = 0
    failed = 0
    best_time = -1.0
    best_name = ""
    for i in range(n):
        parts = input().split()
        status = parts[0]
        name = parts[1]
        t = float(parts[2])
        if status == "OK":
            passed = passed + 1
        else:
            failed = failed + 1
        if t > best_time:
            best_time = t
            best_name = name
    print(f"Total runs: {n}")
    print(f"Passed: {passed}")
    print(f"Failed: {failed}")
    print(f"Slowest: {best_name} ({best_time:.2f}s)")

main()

questions.title: Feature Availability Advisor
questions.description:
A feature advisor tells learners which modern Python features their interpreter supports. The fixed table: fstring exists since 3.6, walrus since 3.8, match since 3.10, typehints since 3.5, pathlib since 3.4. A feature is available only on Python 3 when the minor version is at least the required one; Python 2 supports none of them. An unknown feature name must be reported as unknown.

Input Format:
Line 1: two integers M and m, the interpreter's major and minor version (M is 2 or 3; 0 <= m <= 12). Line 2: n, the number of feature queries. Then n lines, each a feature name from the table (an unknown name may also appear).

Output Format:
For each query print '<feature>: available', '<feature>: missing' or '<feature>: unknown'. Finally print: Checked <n> features on Python <M>.<m>

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 8; M is 2 or 3; 0 <= m <= 12.

fstring: available
walrus: missing
match: missing
Checked 3 features on Python 3.7
questions.sampleoutput2:
fstring: missing
typehints: missing
Checked 2 features on Python 2.7
questions.output1:
match: available
pathlib: available
walrus: available
Checked 3 features on Python 3.10
questions.output2:
decorator: unknown
typehints: available
Checked 2 features on Python 3.12
questions.output3:
pathlib: available
fstring: missing
typehints: missing
walrus: missing
Checked 4 features on Python 3.4
